children: U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East tightened staffing and security measures Saturday after U.S. intelligence warned that Iranian plots targeting Americans had reached "advanced stages."
A memo from Director of National Intelligence
Jay Clayton

said that U.S. agencies collected intelligence indicating Tehran has stepped up efforts to go after U.S. personnel, with the threat picture also touching "certain other countries," according to a report by CNBC.

Diplomatic Tensions Signal Rising Oil Prices
Energy markets have been reacting to the risk of a wider conflict, with Brent crude closing at $116.93 a barrel Friday and U.S. benchmark WTI at $103.44.

Fuel costs have also stayed elevated, with diesel averaging $6.3374 a gallon, about 2.9% below its Sept. 22 peak of $6.5276, based on AAA data. Regular gasoline averaged $4.2957, up roughly 40% from a year ago.
U.S. officials have also taken steps to thin staffing in the region, ordering non-emergency government employees to depart Saudi Arabia earlier this week.
In fighting linked to the Houthis, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by the group that were headed toward Taif and Yanbu, according to the report.

President

Iran’s Mixed Signals On Diplomacy

Even as embassy security was tightened, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remained open to discussions with the U.S. under a deal framework agreed in June and brokered by Pakistan.
Reza Amiri Moghadam
, Iran’s ambassador to Islamabad, said Iran would be ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifted a naval blockade, but said Washington rejected the idea.
Iranian state media later disputed that account. Separately, Iranian Foreign Minister
Abbas Araghchi
said on X that Iran is willing to restart talks, contrasting with Trump’s public message that negotiations are not underway.
